texto:
Vodafone Group reported a loss of €3.6 billion for the six months to September 30, 2026, after cutting the value of its German business by €4.85 billion, according to first-half results for its 2027 financial year published on November 10, 2026. In the same statement the company raised its full-year guidance for both profit and cash flow, and reported the fastest quarterly growth on record for Vodafone Business, the division that sells connectivity, cloud, security and AI services to companies and the public sector.
In Short
Vodafone reported a €3.6 billion first-half loss because of accounting charges, chiefly a €4.85 billion cut to the book value of its German business, even as revenue and underlying profit grew and it raised its forecasts for the year. The split matters for anyone who buys from or competes with Vodafone: its business-services arm, which now sells AI customer-engagement tools to small firms with Google, grew 6.6% in the second quarter, while Germany, its largest market, is still losing broadband and TV customers and faces a court ruling on old price increases. What changes is the mix, with Vodafone leaning harder on business software, AI-based customer care and 2,300 more job cuts in Germany to reach its targets.
A loss built from accounting entries
The headline loss is the product of three large non-cash items. The first and largest is the €4.85 billion impairment of goodwill in Vodafone Germany. According to note 3 of the results announcement, the charge "reflects a significant increase in the discount rate arising from higher yields on German government bond rates and an updated plan of the financial performance of Vodafone Germany." The pre-tax risk-adjusted discount rate used to value the German business rose to 8.0%, from 7.5% at March 31, 2026, and the carrying value of Vodafone Germany has been reduced to a value-in-use estimate of €25.5 billion.
Pilar López, Vodafone's chief financial officer, put most of the charge down to the bond market. "Close to 3/4 of the charge have to do with higher government – German government bond yields, and that impacts the discount rate," she said on the results call, according to a transcript published by Nasdaq. She added that "the impairment has to do with the higher interest rates and the impact of the ECJ," referring to the European Court of Justice ruling on historical German price rises discussed below.
The sensitivity table in the announcement shows how exposed that valuation remains. Before the charge, the recoverable amount of the German business sat €4.9 billion below its carrying value. A further 0.5 percentage point rise in the discount rate would have widened that gap to €6.8 billion, while a two-point cut in projected adjusted EBITDAaL growth would have taken it to €7.5 billion. By PPC Land's calculation, the half-point scenario alone represents roughly €1.9 billion of additional exposure. The company states plainly that higher government bond yields at the next balance sheet date "would, in isolation, give rise to a further impairment charge."
The second item is a €2.2 billion write-down of deferred tax assets in the UK following the buyout of CK Hutchison's stake in VodafoneThree, with a further €235 million remeasurement in Germany. These are accounting adjustments with no current cash tax impact, according to the announcement, since the underlying tax losses and capital allowances continue to be carried forward. Partly offsetting both was a €3.0 billion non-cash gain on the consolidation of Safaricom, the Kenyan operator in which Vodacom took a controlling stake on June 30, 2026.
The effective tax rate was (864.3)%, reflecting a tax charge on a loss before tax, and the loss attributable to owners of the parent reached €4.79 billion. Adjusted basic earnings per share fell to 1.48 eurocents from 6.92 eurocents, which the company attributes to lower investment income; the prior-year period included a €782 million gain on bonds bought back before maturity.
Underneath, revenue and profit grew
Strip away those items and the operating picture moved the other way. Total revenue rose 11.4% to €21.9 billion, helped by the consolidation of Safaricom, the merged VodafoneThree in the UK and Telekom Romania's mobile business, partly offset by adverse currency movements. On an organic basis, which removes acquisitions, disposals and currency effects, revenue grew 4.7%.
Service revenue, the recurring income from customers that telecom investors watch most closely, rose 12.8% to €18.4 billion, or 5.8% organically. The quarterly figures show acceleration: organic growth was 5.2% in the first quarter and 6.4% in the second. On the call, according to the Nasdaq transcript, chief executive Margherita Della Valle described the second-quarter rate as "the highest in 3 years." In Vodafone's own results video, López called it "one of our highest ever growth rates."
Adjusted EBITDAaL - Vodafone's preferred profit measure, which treats lease costs as an operating expense - rose 12.6% to €6.45 billion, and 6.4% organically. The margin improved 0.5 percentage points on an organic basis to 29.5%. Quarterly, the margin moved from 28.5% in the first quarter to 30.4% in the second, according to the segment tables.
The table below sets out the main group figures for the half, as reported in the results announcement.
Net debt at March 31, 2026 was €25,411 million; the comparison in the table is with September 30, 2025.

"I am very happy about our overall Group performance, but Germany is not yet where it needs to be," Della Valle said in the announcement. "We have a clear action plan in progress, which is structurally simplifying our German operations and improving customer satisfaction across all of our services."
Guidance moves up again
The November 10 statement raises both FY27 ranges for the second time, after a July update that added Safaricom; the full bridge is set out below. At the mid-points, the company says the new ranges imply organic growth of 7% in adjusted EBITDAaL and 21% in adjusted free cash flow. The European outlook, set at €7.6-7.9 billion of adjusted EBITDAaL, is unchanged. According to the Nasdaq transcript, an analyst at JPMorgan, Akhil Dattani, noted that the upper end of the old ranges is now the mid-point of the new ones. López said the UK and Germany had performed well enough to absorb the €100 million hit from the court ruling in Germany while keeping the European outlook intact.
Restructuring and integration costs in FY27 are expected to peak at about €0.7 billion, including about €0.4 billion tied to the VodafoneThree merger.
How the FY27 guidance is built, step by step
The results announcement sets out the bridge from last year's reported figures to the upgraded ranges. In the order the document gives them, the steps for adjusted EBITDAaL and adjusted free cash flow are:
- FY26 actual, reported basis: €11.4 billion adjusted EBITDAaL; €2.6 billion adjusted free cash flow.
- Impact of exchange rates: minus €0.1 billion on each measure.
- Remove impact of Türkiye hyperinflation accounting: plus €0.1 billion on adjusted EBITDAaL; nil on cash flow.
- Impact of M&A transactions (the disposal of VodafoneZiggo): nil on adjusted EBITDAaL; minus €0.1 billion on cash flow.
- FY26 re-based at FY27 guidance exchange rates: €11.4 billion and €2.4 billion.
- Growth: €0.5-0.8 billion and €0.2-0.5 billion, giving the original FY27 guidance of €11.9-12.2 billion and €2.6-2.9 billion.
- Nine-month FY27 Safaricom consolidation impact: plus €1.1 billion on adjusted EBITDAaL; nil on cash flow, giving the July guidance of €13.0-13.3 billion and €2.6-2.9 billion.
- Upgraded FY27 guidance: €13.2-13.4 billion and €2.8-3.0 billion, with implied organic growth of about 6% to 8% and about 17% to 25%.
The guidance excludes hyperinflation accounting in Türkiye and is set at exchange rates of €1 to GBP 0.87, ZAR 19.60, TRY 53.07, EGP 62.53 and KES 159.66. In the announcement's words, "The guidance assumes no material change to the structure of the Group." A footnote adds that the Safaricom transaction "is subject to a legal challenge."
Vodafone Business posts its best quarter
For marketers and agencies, the most consequential line in the release may not be Germany at all. It is Vodafone Business, which reported organic service revenue growth of 5.8% in the first half and 6.6% in the second quarter, described by the company as its best-ever growth. According to the additional-information spreadsheet, quarterly Business service revenue reached €2.32 billion in the second quarter, up from €2.10 billion in the first, and €4.41 billion across the half, a reported increase of 10.6%. By PPC Land's calculation, Business now accounts for about 24% of Group service revenue.
Growth came from what Vodafone calls digital services: Internet of Things connectivity, cloud and security services, software-defined networks, and digital solutions and communications. According to the results presentation, digital services grew 19.7% in the first half, with software-as-a-service revenue up 80.4% and cloud and security revenue up 13.2%. Digital services now make up 27.8% of Business service revenue, 3.1 percentage points more than a year earlier. Growth in the European digital portfolio reached 25.8% in the second quarter, against 20.5% for the group.
Over the twelve months to September, digital services generated €2.4 billion in revenue, according to the presentation's product breakdown:
The four digital lines in the chart add up to €2.3 billion, by PPC Land's calculation, against the €2.4 billion the slide states, a gap consistent with rounding. The company counts 5 million business customers and 267 million connected IoT devices.
"Vodafone Business delivered its highest-ever service revenue growth of 6.6% in Q2, as our digital services portfolio is now growing more than 20% year on year," López said in Vodafone's results video.
AI concierge, sovereign cloud and data centres
The product list behind those numbers reaches into territory that marketers know well. In partnership with Google, Vodafone launched AI concierge, which the announcement describes as "a customer engagement and productivity solution for small businesses." Della Valle was more specific in the video: "This year, we have launched new AI services for SMEs through our AI Concierge that allows businesses to automate customer interactions and improve productivity."
The company has also expanded managed cyber security for small and mid-sized businesses from Germany to Portugal, Ireland and Romania, with dedicated security operations centres in those four countries. In Germany, it was named the exclusive telecom partner for Amazon Web Services' sovereign cloud solution, a step that puts Vodafone between enterprise buyers and a hyperscaler that has been signing European partners for its sovereign cloud since at least April. In April, PPC Land reported that euNetworks became the first connectivity partner of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, a facility designed to keep data and operations within the EU.
Vodafone's physical footprint is following the same logic. According to the presentation, the group holds a 30% stake in an Egyptian joint venture with El Sewedy Electric and Cassava Technologies, with 20MW of initial and 200MW of planned capacity, and is separately developing what it calls Egypt's first sovereign AI data centre. Safaricom operates two central data centres in Kenya and Ethiopia with 9.1MW of current and 35MW of planned capacity, which the company says will provide GPU-as-a-service. In Türkiye, a 50:50 joint venture with DAMAC Digital opened the group's sixth sovereign data centre in Izmir in September 2026, with an initial US$100 million investment, 4MW of capacity rising to 20MW, and agreements already covering more than half that capacity.
"These aren't standalone products," Della Valle said in the video. "They're examples of how Vodafone is evolving from a connectivity provider into a broader technology partner for our business customers to help them operate, compete and grow in a digital world."
Germany's B2B turn
The German business illustrates the shift. Vodafone Germany's Business service revenue grew 3.7% organically in the first half, as demand for SaaS and cloud and security services offset pressure in core connectivity. On the call, Della Valle said digital services in Germany grew 30% in the first half. Asked how large the segment is, she offered approximate figures: "imagine roughly 25% of the revenues in Germany from B2B and 25% or a little bit more of the B2B revenues coming from digital services," according to the Nasdaq transcript. She also said Skaylink, the cloud services company Vodafone acquired in December 2025, had "already signed over 100 contracts with Vodafone customers" over the last two quarters.
There is a cost attached. According to the announcement, Germany saw "an increase in variable costs from Business digital services growth," one of the factors that weighed on the country's profit.
Germany: broadband prices, a court and 2,300 roles
Germany generates 30% of group service revenue and 33% of adjusted EBITDAaL, so its weakness carries weight. Service revenue rose 1.1% to €5.48 billion, but organic growth was only 0.4%, and turned negative in the second quarter at minus 0.5%, after 1.2% in the first. Mobile service revenue declined 0.4% over the half and 1.9% in the second quarter, as the prior year included higher wholesale income from the migration of 1&1's customers onto Vodafone's 5G network. Adjusted EBITDAaL fell 3.2% organically to €2.14 billion, and the margin dropped 1.2 percentage points to 35.3%.
About two percentage points of that EBITDAaL decline came from a single source: a legal provision linked to price increases of €5 a month that Vodafone Germany applied to fixed-line customers in 2023. According to the announcement, that decision was "partly based upon its interpretation of the contract amendment provisions in the German Telecommunications Code ('Telekommunikationsgesetz') which appeared to recognise that providers could reserve a unilateral amendment right in their terms where customers were given a cost-free right to terminate." The consumer federation's class action alleges that "terms regarding price increases in the consumer contracts entered into by Vodafone Germany's customers up until August 2023 are invalid under German civil law."
That reading no longer holds. In September 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union issued its judgment "deciding that the Directive does not create itself a unilateral right to change the terms of a consumer contract." Following that judgment, Vodafone says it has "ceased recognising the revenue associated with the historical €5 per month price increases for the 2.5 million broadband customers still on legacy contracts." By PPC Land's calculation, €5 a month across 2.5 million customers amounts to up to €150 million a year, if all those contracts remained in place. The presentation puts the second-quarter impact on German service revenue at minus 0.3 percentage points, "with full impact from Q3."
Two court dates follow. In the injunction proceedings brought by the Federation of German Consumer Organisations (vzbv), the Higher Regional Court of Düsseldorf heard the case on November 3, 2026, and its decision is scheduled for publication on November 26, 2026; according to the announcement, the court has indicated it will grant the injunction on the basis that the contract term is invalid. In the separate class action at the Higher Regional Court of Hamm, about 118,500 customers had registered by September 30, 2026, and a hearing is scheduled for November 3, 2027. On the call, according to the Nasdaq transcript, López said the class action is not expected to conclude "at best" before late calendar 2027, and confirmed the provision is not included in this year's cash flow guidance.
Customers leave as prices rise
The customer numbers show the trade-off Vodafone is making. The German broadband base shrank by 198,000 in the half, including 119,000 customers on its gigabit network, a decline the company attributes to "our focus on value optimisation." Broadband ARPU from new customers rose 25% year on year (30% in the first quarter, 20% in the second). The base stood at 9.72 million at the end of September, according to the spreadsheet, down from 10.07 million a year earlier.
TV continues to fall. Vodafone lost 115,000 TV customers in the half, leaving 8.62 million, and the company cites "the structural decline in demand for standalone linear TV services." The presentation estimates the TV decline cost German service revenue about one percentage point. Mobile contract customers declined by 75,000 over the half, including 34,000 Business disconnections, although the second quarter showed a net gain of 10,000. Vodafone connected a further 5.5 million IoT devices in Germany, driven by demand from carmakers.
There is a commercial dispute tied to the TV business as well. In August 2026, four teleshopping channels filed a claim against Vodafone Germany at the Munich Regional Court, alleging breaches of competition law in relation to "the commercial model for determining the charges applied to TV channels for providing access to broadband cable networks." The claimants seek about €239 million in damages for overpaid fees and lost profits, plus an injunction. Vodafone's defence is due in April 2027; the company says it believes "it is probable that no present obligation exists." A separate Federal Cartel Office investigation, triggered by a complaint from 1&1 over delayed tower sites, remains open, with a Düsseldorf hearing on a procedural challenge scheduled for January 2027.
Asked about new mobile entrants including Revolut, Della Valle said, according to the Nasdaq transcript: "Net-net, I think nothing is materially changing in the pricing environment in Germany." Competition in the German market has nonetheless reached unusual places. On the day before Vodafone's results, PPC Land reported that a Cologne court had banned a Deutsche Telekom campaign that replaced the network name on customers' phones with the slogan "Im besten Netz".
Convergence as the counterweight
Vodafone's case for Germany rests on selling more products to each household. According to the presentation, the company has 12.8 million single-product households in Germany, 24% of broadband customers and 19% of mobile customers are classed as converged. Net Promoter Scores improved by four points year on year across consumer, mobile, TV and cable products. The company says expanded AI care capabilities raised first-contact resolution to about 80% of customer enquiries. Network data points include 5G standalone coverage of more than 94% of the population and a gigabit footprint of 31.5 million households, with the OXG fibre joint venture at 1.1 million homes passed and a target of 1.4 million by March 2027.
On November 9, Vodafone Germany announced about 2,300 role reductions over the next two financial years. PPC Land reported that the restructuring folds customer service into the consumer and business sales units and widens the use of AI, which the German release said creates and steers advertising campaigns. The results announcement adds a financial frame: the group expects to recognise a restructuring provision in the second half, and the plan sits within the roughly €0.7 billion of restructuring and integration costs already expected for FY27. According to the Nasdaq transcript, Della Valle said the cuts mean "we will have reduced headcount in Germany by 40% since we began our transformation."
"While I'm very pleased with our overall performance, our financial performance in Germany over the last few years has been disappointing. But we have not stood still," Della Valle said in the video.
The UK: SuperMobile, Vodafone TV and leaner marketing
Vodafone has owned all of VodafoneThree since July 2026, when it completed the purchase of CK Hutchison Group Telecom Holding's 49% stake for £4.3 billion (€5.0 billion). The UK business reported organic service revenue growth of 0.9% and organic adjusted EBITDAaL growth of 5.9% to €984 million, with a margin of 20.3%.
The synergy targets have gone up. At the VodafoneThree Investor Briefing in October 2026, the company raised its annual cost and capex synergy target to £0.8 billion by FY30, from £0.7 billion, and introduced a £1 billion annual saving target by FY32. It also set a goal for operating free cash flow to more than triple by FY32 against FY25. Over €50 million of cost synergies were delivered in the first half, with about €100 million expected in the second half, according to the presentation.
Marketing sits close to the centre of those savings. The presentation lists "retail footprint integration," "marketing & logistics savings" and "integration of teams" as the key cost synergies of the half. Elsewhere it records that 42% of stores are now multi-brand following retail consolidation, alongside "rationalisation of marketing and logistics activities." The UK profit bridge also notes that synergy gains were partly offset by "phasing of marketing spend in the prior year."
On the product side, Vodafone launched SuperMobile in September 2026, a tariff that sells access to its 5G standalone network with higher speeds and guaranteed minimum speeds. "In a UK first, we have guaranteed minimum speeds for our SuperMobile customers. We've been really encouraged by the early response, with the majority of new iPhone customers choosing SuperMobile," Della Valle said in the video. Vodafone 5G speeds have risen 82% since April 2025, according to the announcement, which cites Ookla Speedtest Intelligence; the presentation's chart shows the national average 5G download speed climbing from 172 Mbps in mid-2025 to 313 Mbps. In October 2026, Vodafone launched Vodafone TV for consumer customers in the UK, a move it presents as a way to deepen engagement and retention.
Customer counts were mixed. The mobile contract base declined by 62,000 in the half, including the disconnection of 40,000 "very low value Business SIMs." The prepaid brands VOXI and SMARTY added 166,000 customers, broadband grew by 76,000 and fixed wireless access by 54,000. Consumer contract churn fell 0.6 percentage points year on year, according to the announcement. The presentation counts 28 million UK mobile customers, including 6.6 million who take only a single Vodafone mobile product, a pool it calls a convergence opportunity. Only 7% of UK mobile customers are converged, against 40% of broadband customers.
AI in customer care and in the cost base
Della Valle described AI as central both to customer experience and to cost reduction. "Our TOBi chatbot handles over one million customer interactions every single day, almost half a billion per year, with a resolution rate of 85% and strong impact on customer satisfaction," she said in the video. (One million a day would amount to 365 million a year, by PPC Land's calculation; the half-billion figure implies closer to 1.37 million a day.) She added: "Germany is the first of our markets where AI-enabled agent-assist tools are now supporting customer service requests, helping improve customer satisfaction even further."
Vodafone now says it holds Net Promoter Score leadership or co-leadership in 12 markets. The presentation reports a 10% improvement in the "promoter-to-detractor" sentiment mix and a 2.0 percentage point improvement in customer loyalty, measured by year-on-year changes in mobile churn across all markets.
The same tools appear in the cost programme. In May 2026, Vodafone committed to more than €2 billion of annual gross opex savings across Europe and its shared operations by FY30, translating into more than €1 billion of annual net savings. The company describes this as a cut of 30% of its addressable opex base, more than 20% of FY26 European and shared-operations opex, which the presentation puts at €9.4 billion. The net figure equals more than 10% of the €7.5 billion of FY26 European and shared-operations adjusted EBITDAaL. On the call, López put it at 13% of European EBITDA, according to the Nasdaq transcript, a different base.
"Across the Group we are simplifying processes, increasing automation, expanding the use of AI and leveraging the benefits of our scaled shared platforms. These activities have given us the confidence to target a reduction of 30% of our addressable spend," Della Valle said in the video.
The first half delivered more than €200 million of gross savings, about 10% of the target, including €50 million of UK synergies and about 3,000 role reductions across Europe and shared operations. That comes on top of 11,000 role reductions between FY23 and FY26. Among the AI examples in the presentation: insourced software development cutting time-to-market and cost "by up to 80%," a "self-healing" international network agent and AI involvement in more than 99% of tenders. Vodafone expects a net reduction in European opex of more than €200 million in FY27. "EUR 1 billion to the bottom line in Europe and roughly 1/4 of that will be delivered on the first year of the plan," Della Valle said, according to the Nasdaq transcript. The company also flags headwinds from inflation in employment costs, towers and energy.
Africa and Türkiye carry the growth
Africa now provides 24% of group service revenue and 32% of adjusted EBITDAaL. Service revenue rose 41.5% to €4.50 billion with Safaricom consolidated from July 1, 2026, and organic growth was 13.4%. Organic adjusted EBITDAaL rose 18.0% and the margin reached 37.9%.
Financial services drove a large share of that growth. M-Pesa revenue at Safaricom rose 13.7% organically to €669 million, M-Pesa revenue in Vodacom's international markets rose 23.4% to €285 million, and Vodafone Cash in Egypt grew 74.3% to €113 million, now 10.1% of Egyptian service revenue, with 16.7 million users. The presentation counts 108 million financial services customers and 2.2 million merchants across the region, with Africa's fintech revenue up 19% to €1.2 billion in the half. In the video, Della Valle said Egyptian service revenue "grew 36% in the first half, supported by continued customer growth, strong demand for data and financial services expansion: Vodafone Cash is growing rapidly, with revenue up over 74% and 17 million customers."
The Safaricom deal remains contested. Vodacom acquired 15% from the Government of Kenya for KES 204 billion (€1.4 billion) and 5% from Vodafone for KES 68 billion (€0.5 billion), lifting its holding to 55%. On September 15, 2026, Kenya's High Court declared the transaction null and void; on October 13, the Court of Appeal in Nairobi ordered that the status quo be maintained pending its decision. On the call, Della Valle said the appeal has been "fast tracked for urgent resolution," according to the Nasdaq transcript.
The consolidation reshapes Vodafone's customer count. According to the spreadsheet, the group had 361.3 million mobile customers at the end of September, against 279.3 million three months earlier; Safaricom alone accounted for 79.0 million. Across Africa the figure is 255.5 million.
In Türkiye, organic service revenue rose 32.8% and organic adjusted EBITDAaL 32.7%, figures that exclude hyperinflation accounting and currency translation. In euro terms, excluding hyperinflation adjustments, service revenue rose 12.7%. Vodafone Türkiye launched 5G in April 2026 and reports more than 7 million 5G customers. The company says its loyalty platform, Vodafone Happy, received more than 300 million visits in its first year, and customer loyalty improved 13.0 percentage points year on year.
Other Europe, which covers Portugal, Ireland, Greece, Romania, the Czech Republic and Albania, grew organic service revenue 1.4% while organic adjusted EBITDAaL fell 4.6%, due to a legal one-off in Portugal in the prior year. Greek Business revenue benefited from public-sector projects funded through the European Recovery and Resilience Facility, which closed in September 2026; the presentation describes these as the last such projects.
Cash, debt and the dividend
Adjusted free cash flow was an outflow of €440 million, a €143 million improvement on the prior year, as higher adjusted EBITDAaL and lower working capital outflows more than offset higher capital additions, taxes and dividends paid to minority shareholders after the Safaricom deal.
Net debt climbed to €33.5 billion from €25.4 billion at March 31, 2026. The €8.1 billion increase includes €5.0 billion for the VodafoneThree buyout, €1.38 billion for the additional Safaricom stake and €537 million of net debt acquired with Safaricom. Leverage, measured as net debt to adjusted EBITDAaL with a pro forma full year of Safaricom, rose to 2.5x from 2.3x a year earlier, within the target range of 2.25-2.75x. Cash and short-term investments totalled €8.4 billion.
Vodafone completed the sale of its VodafoneZiggo interest to Liberty Global on July 31, 2026, for €1.0 billion in cash and a 10% stake in Ziggo Group. As part of that deal, Vodafone will keep providing services, including brand licensing, to VodafoneZiggo, with expected charges of €625 million over the next ten years.
The interim dividend rose 2.5% to 2.306 eurocents per share. Under the policy stated in the announcement, "The interim dividend is set at 50% of the prior full year dividend." The ex-dividend date is November 19, 2026 for ordinary shareholders and November 20 for ADR holders, with payment scheduled for February 3, 2027.
A shareholder question left open
One topic surfaced only in the analyst questions. James Ratzer of New Street Research asked about Xavier Niel's planned entry to the share register and possible board representation, putting the voting rights involved at just under 20%, according to the Nasdaq transcript. Della Valle declined to engage on specifics. "We never comment on engagement with individual shareholders. But in this particular case, the share transfer is still not approved," she said, adding that regulatory processes remain open, "particularly the NSIA process in the U.K." The results announcement and video do not mention the matter.
Why this matters for the marketing community
Telecom operators matter to advertisers in at least three ways: as heavy advertisers themselves, as owners of customer data and distribution, and increasingly as vendors of the software that small businesses use to talk to their own customers.
On the first count, Vodafone's plans include savings in marketing itself. The UK synergy plan explicitly includes marketing rationalisation and retail consolidation, and the German restructuring announced on November 9 names creating and steering ad campaigns among the tasks AI performs. Vodafone has changed how it buys media before: in July 2025, PPC Land reported that the company increased the news inventory available to its ads by 10% after revising its brand suitability approach with DoubleVerify. Across the Atlantic, operators continue to spend heavily; T-Mobile's advertising expense rose 5.5% to $956 million in the third quarter of 2026.
On the second, Vodafone is one of the founding operators behind Utiq, the identity service built on carrier data. The European Commission cleared the four-operator joint venture of Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone in February 2023, Utiq launched in the UK through Virgin Media O2 and Vodafone in June 2025 and reported 70 million users across six European markets in November 2025. A group with 361 million mobile customers, 18.8 million broadband customers and 11.1 million European TV customers controls distribution and customer signals that matter to advertisers, from cable TV in Germany to identity through Utiq. It also controls how traffic reaches those customers: in November 2025, Vodafone withdrew from public internet exchanges in Germany, moving peering to a single partner.
The third count is the newest. AI concierge, sold with Google to small businesses to "automate customer interactions," puts Vodafone into the same space as the AI receptionists and messaging tools that martech vendors sell, with the distribution advantage of an existing billing relationship with 5 million business customers. SaaS revenue of €0.4 billion over twelve months is small next to €6.2 billion from core connectivity, but it grew 80.4% in the half. FreeCast's chief executive argued in August that attention, not fibre, is a telecom company's most valuable asset. Vodafone's first half points to a different emphasis: the business customer relationship, with software layered on top.
What the documents do not say
Vodafone gives no pricing, customer count or model details for AI concierge, no marketing or advertising expense, no share of German campaigns made with AI and no split of the 3,000 role reductions by function, and none of its documents mentions Utiq or advertising revenue. The 36% Egyptian and 30% German digital growth rates cited by Della Valle do not appear in the announcement's tables.
Key facts
- Company: Vodafone Group Plc, registered in England No. 1833679; registered office Vodafone House, The Connection, Newbury, Berkshire RG14 2FN. Traded in the US as NASDAQ: VOD.
- Reporting period: H1 FY27, the six months to September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27 covers July to September 2026). The financial year ends March 31, 2027.

Summary
Who: Vodafone Group Plc, led by chief executive Margherita Della Valle and chief financial officer Pilar López, with its German, UK, African and Turkish operations and its Vodafone Business division.
What: First-half FY27 results showing a €3.6 billion loss, driven by a €4.85 billion goodwill impairment in Germany and a €2.2 billion UK deferred tax write-down, partly offset by a €3.0 billion Safaricom gain. Underlying service revenue grew 5.8% organically, adjusted EBITDAaL 6.4%, and Vodafone Business posted best-ever quarterly growth of 6.6%, with digital services up 19.7%. FY27 guidance rose to €13.2-13.4 billion adjusted EBITDAaL and €2.8-3.0 billion adjusted free cash flow.
When: Published November 10, 2026, covering the six months to September 30, 2026. Court decisions in Germany are scheduled for November 26, 2026 and November 3, 2027; the interim dividend is scheduled for payment on February 3, 2027.
Where: Group-wide, with Germany, the UK, Africa (including Kenya, Egypt and South Africa), Türkiye and six other European markets.
Why: Higher German government bond yields and a revised German business plan, including the effect of a European Court of Justice ruling on historical price increases, cut the value of Vodafone Germany. At the same time, growth in Africa, Türkiye and business digital services, UK merger synergies and a cost programme built partly on AI lifted underlying profit and allowed the company to raise its forecasts.
